primitives.name: Product Space Measurability
primitives.verbatim_quote: A subset of Xi-1 Xi will be called measurable if it belongs to the σ-ring S (which is in fact a σ-algebra) generated by the class of all measurable rectangles; we shall write S = Xi-1 Si.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'Xi': 'Index set of topological spaces', 'Si': 'σ-algebra on Xi', 'S': 'Product σ-algebra on ∏Xi'}
primitives.assumptions: Each Xi is a measurable space with associated σ-algebra Si.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the product involves uncountably many factors without finite support.

layer2.mapping: The product σ-algebra S on ∏Xi is isomorphic to the tensor product of individual σ-algebras {Si}.
layer2.telemetry: Measurable rectangle cardinality in finite projections determines full-space measurability.

primitives.name: J-Cylinder Invariance
primitives.verbatim_quote: A set E in X is called a J-cylinder if x ≡ y (J) implies that x and y belong or do not belong to E simultaneously.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'J': 'Finite subset of positive integers', 'x, y': 'Points in product space X', 'E': 'Subset of X'}
primitives.assumptions: J ⊆ I where I is the set of positive integers; x ≡ y(J) iff xj = yj for all j ∈ J.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When J is infinite or when the coordinate-wise agreement fails due to non-measurability.

layer2.mapping: J-cylinders form a sub-σ-algebra of S, closed under complementation and countable union.
layer2.telemetry: Coordinate invariance under finite index sets defines kernel structure for conditional independence.

primitives.name: Finite-Dimensional Projection
primitives.verbatim_quote: If J = {1, · · ., n} and if a subset E cf X is a [measurable] J-cylinder, then E = A × X(n), where A is a [measurable] subset of X1 ×·.·× Xn.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'A': 'Measurable subset of X1 × · · · × Xn', 'X(n)': 'Product space ∏i>n Xi', 'E': 'J-cylinder in X'}
primitives.assumptions: J = {1, ..., n} is finite; E is measurable and J-cylindrical.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When J includes infinitely many indices or when E lacks cylindrical structure.

layer2.mapping: Finite-dimensional projection maps J-cylinders bijectively onto Cartesian products of measurable sets.
layer2.telemetry: Projection dimensionality determines marginal distribution compatibility in probabilistic models.

The foundational structure of product spaces arises from the need to generalize measure theory to infinite-dimensional settings. The σ-algebra S generated by measurable rectangles ensures that operations like integration and probability can be consistently defined over infinite products. The concept of J-cylinders introduces a key abstraction: sets that remain unchanged under modifications of coordinates outside a finite index set J. This property allows for the decomposition of complex sets into simpler, finite-dimensional components. For example, if J = {1,...,n}, then a J-cylinder E corresponds exactly to a Cartesian product A × X(n), where A is measurable in the finite-dimensional base space. This duality between finite-dimensional projections and infinite product structures enables rigorous treatment of stochastic processes indexed by natural numbers. The failure mode occurs when attempting to apply these constructions to uncountable index sets or when the underlying spaces lack sufficient structure for σ-algebra generation. These primitives provide the theoretical backbone for Bayesian inference in high-dimensional or infinite-dimensional domains, particularly in modeling sequential data or continuous-time systems.
